passages.t: A greeting, and thanks for what Epaphras planted
passages.happening:
“Paul, an apostle of Christ Jesus by the will of God, and Timothy our brother, To the saints and faithful brothers in Christ at Colossae: Grace and peace to you from God our Father” (verses 1-2).

Paul thanks God for them, “because we have heard about your faith in Christ Jesus and your love for all the saints” (verse 4), which spring from “the hope stored up for you in heaven” (verse 5). The gospel “is bearing fruit and growing” all over the world, just as it has among them (verse 6).

And he names the one who brought it: “You learned it from Epaphras, our beloved fellow servant, who is a faithful minister of Christ on our behalf, and who also informed us of your love in the Spirit” (verses 7-8).
passages.hearers:
Paul had never met these people (2:1). So he begins by saying what he has heard, and it is good. They trust Christ. They love all the saints, not only their friends. And both come from their hope, which is safe in heaven.

Faith, love and hope: Paul often puts these three together (1 Corinthians 13:13). Here hope comes first in the order of causes. Because they know what God has kept for them, they can trust him now and love others freely.

Notice the words ‘bearing fruit and growing’. The gospel is alive. It grows like a plant, in Colossae and ‘all over the world’. A small church in a small town is part of something very large.

And notice Epaphras. He was one of their own (4:12). He did not just pass on information; he taught them, and they ‘truly understood the grace of God’ (verse 6). Paul calls him ‘fellow servant’, the same word as slave, and ‘faithful minister’. Paul gives the credit for this church to someone else, gladly. As the next chapter will show, some new teachers were saying the Colossians needed something more than what Epaphras taught them. Paul's first move is to say that what they received was the real gospel.
passages.ot:
‘Bearing fruit and growing’ echoes God's first blessing on human beings: “Be fruitful and multiply, and fill the earth” (Genesis 1:28). The gospel is God's new creation, spreading as the first creation was meant to.

Isaiah says God's word grows like rain-watered seed: “so My word that proceeds from My mouth will not return to Me empty, but it will accomplish what I please” (Isaiah 55:11).
passages.asks: Paul thanks God for faith, love and hope that he heard about from someone else. Ask what others would hear about your faith and love. Ask who your Epaphras was, the person who first taught you the gospel, and whether you have thanked God for them. And ask whether you are content with the gospel you received, or keep looking for something more.

passages.t: A prayer to be filled, and rescued into the Son's kingdom
passages.happening:
Paul tells them what he prays: that God will “fill you with the knowledge of His will in all spiritual wisdom and understanding, so that you may walk in a manner worthy of the Lord and may please Him in every way” (verses 9-10). He prays that they will bear fruit, grow in knowing God, be strengthened “so that you may have full endurance and patience” (verse 11), and give thanks joyfully.

The reason for thanks: the Father “has qualified you to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light. He has rescued us from the dominion of darkness and brought us into the kingdom of His beloved Son, in whom we have redemption, the forgiveness of sins” (verses 12-14).
passages.hearers:
‘Fill’ is a key word in this letter. Some were telling the Colossians that they needed a fuller spiritual life, through special knowledge and experiences. Paul prays that they will be filled, but with the knowledge of God's will, and that this knowledge will show up in how they live. For Paul, knowing God is never only in the head. It walks.

Notice what the strength is for: ‘endurance and patience’. Not great feats, but the power to keep going and to bear with people.

Then comes a picture the Colossians would know from Israel's story, even as Gentiles. God rescued Israel from Egypt and gave each tribe a share of the promised land as its ‘inheritance’. Now God has rescued them from a dark kingdom and moved them into another one, the kingdom of his Son. The word for ‘brought’ means to move from one place to another, and some readers hear in it the way ancient kings moved whole peoples to new lands. Either way, they have changed countries.

And the first gift of the new kingdom is ‘redemption, the forgiveness of sins’. Redemption means being bought out of slavery. Here it is defined simply: forgiveness.
passages.ot:
The rescue is the exodus told again. God said to Israel, “I will bring you out from under the yoke of the Egyptians and deliver you from their bondage. I will redeem you with an outstretched arm” (Exodus 6:6). And Moses sang, “With loving devotion You will lead the people You have redeemed” (Exodus 15:13).

The inheritance recalls the land shared among Israel's tribes, and the psalm that says the best share is God himself: “The LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; You have made my lot secure” (Psalm 16:5).

And the move from darkness to light is Isaiah's promise: “The people walking in darkness have seen a great light” (Isaiah 9:2).
passages.asks: Paul prays for knowledge that walks, and strength that endures. Ask whether what you know about God has reached how you live. Ask where you need patience more than power. And give thanks, as Paul does, that you have been moved into a new kingdom and forgiven.

passages.t: The song of Christ: over creation and over the new creation
passages.happening:
Now the great song. It has two halves.

Christ and creation: “The Son is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn over all creation. For in Him all things were created, things in heaven and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities. All things were created through Him and for Him. He is before all things, and in Him all things hold together” (verses 15-17).

Christ and the new creation: “And He is the head of the body, the church; He is the beginning and firstborn from among the dead, so that in all things He may have preeminence. For God was pleased to have all His fullness dwell in Him, and through Him to reconcile to Himself all things, whether things on earth or things in heaven, by making peace through the blood of His cross” (verses 18-20).
passages.hearers:
Many scholars think these verses are an early Christian hymn that Paul quotes or shapes; others think he wrote them himself. Either way, the two halves match. Both use ‘firstborn’. Both speak of ‘all things’. The one who made everything is the one who makes everything new.

‘Image of the invisible God’ means that in the Son the God no one can see is made visible. If you want to know what God is like, look at Jesus.

The Colossians lived among people who feared unseen powers. ‘Thrones or dominions or rulers or authorities’ were names for such powers, in heaven or on earth. Paul says every one of them was made through Christ and for him. Nothing the Colossians feared stood outside his rule.

‘In Him all things hold together’ means the world does not hold itself together. The Son keeps it in being, moment by moment.

Then the second half. Christ is the head of the church, and the first to rise from the dead, never to die again. And God reconciles all things through him, not by force, but ‘by making peace through the blood of His cross’. The one who holds the universe together was nailed to a Roman cross, and that is how God makes peace.
passages.ot:
God made human beings in his image: “Let Us make man in Our image, after Our likeness” (Genesis 1:26). Christ is the true image, the one who shows God perfectly.

‘Firstborn’ in Israel meant the heir with first place. God says of David's royal heir, “I will indeed appoint him as My firstborn, the highest of the kings of the earth” (Psalm 89:27).

Israel praised God for making the world by his wisdom: “He established the world by His wisdom and stretched out the heavens by His understanding” (Jeremiah 10:12). “How many are Your works, O LORD! In wisdom You have made them all” (Psalm 104:24). The song says that wisdom, through which God made all things, has a name: the Son.
passages.hard:
‘The firstborn over all creation.’ Does this mean the Son was the first thing God created?

No. In Israel the firstborn was the heir, the one with first place, and God could call someone ‘firstborn’ who was not born first, as Psalm 89:27 shows. And the very next words rule out the idea that the Son is a creature: ‘For in Him all things were created’. All things were made through him. He is not one of the things made. He is the one through whom they were made, and ‘He is before all things’.

The church confesses this. The Nicene Creed confesses the Son as ‘begotten, not made, being of one substance with the Father; by whom all things were made’. John says the same: “Through Him all things were made, and without Him nothing was made that has been made” (John 1:3).

In the 300s a teacher named Arius taught that the Son was the first and greatest of God's creatures, glorious but made. Some have read ‘firstborn over all creation’ that way, and some still do. The church, at the Council of Nicaea in 325 and after, said that this teaching is outside the Christian faith, because if the Son is a creature, then God did not come to save us himself. These notes say the same, plainly and gently, with no contempt for any person who has been taught otherwise. This is not a question on which faithful Christians differ. It is the confession of the whole church.
passages.asks: The song says that everything was made through Christ, holds together in him, and is reconciled by his cross. Ask what you are afraid of, and whether it stands outside his rule. Ask whether you know God by looking at Jesus. And ask what it would mean for him to have first place in your life, not only in creation.

passages.t: Reconciled, if you continue in the faith
passages.happening:
Paul turns the song to the Colossians themselves. “Once you were alienated from God and were hostile in your minds, engaging in evil deeds” (verse 21). “But now He has reconciled you by Christ’s physical body through death to present you holy, unblemished, and blameless in His presence” (verse 22).

Then a condition: “if indeed you continue in your faith, established and firm, not moved from the hope of the gospel you heard” (verse 23). It is the gospel “which has been proclaimed to every creature under heaven, and of which I, Paul, have become a servant” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
The great words about ‘all things’ now come down to ‘you’. The God who is reconciling the universe has reconciled these Gentile believers in a small town.

Notice what they were: not only far off, but ‘hostile in your minds’. The problem was not just bad behaviour. It was a mind turned against God. Reconciliation means enemies made friends.

Notice how: ‘by Christ’s physical body through death’. The new teaching was hard on the body (2:23). Paul insists that God saved them through a real body, really dying on a cross.

And notice the goal: to stand before God ‘holy, unblemished, and blameless’, words used of a sacrifice with no defect. That is how God will see them, because of Christ.

Then the ‘if’. Paul is not unsure about God. He is warning them not to be moved by the new teaching. Real faith keeps holding on to the gospel it first heard.
passages.ot:
The prophets named the problem: “But your iniquities have built barriers between you and your God, and your sins have hidden His face from you” (Isaiah 59:2). Reconciliation tears down that barrier.

They also promised a cleansing only God could give: “I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean. I will cleanse you from all your impurities and all your idols” (Ezekiel 36:25).

And the psalm says how far God's forgiveness goes: “As far as the east is from the west, so far has He removed our transgressions from us” (Psalm 103:12).
passages.hard:
‘If indeed you continue in your faith.’ Does this mean a believer could lose their salvation?

Christians read verses like this in different ways. Some, in the Reformed and Baptist traditions, hold that those God truly saves will continue in faith, kept by God, so that continuing is the sign of real faith, not the price of keeping it. Others, in the Wesleyan, Arminian, Catholic and Orthodox traditions, hold that a believer can turn away and fall from grace, so the warning is real. These notes do not choose. The note on Romans 8:31-39 and the Honest Answer ‘Can you lose your salvation?’ set out the views.

All agree that the warning is meant to keep believers holding on to Christ, not to make them anxious about whether they have held on well enough. The same passage says that Christ has already reconciled them and will present them blameless.

If you are a person whose conscience never rests, who keeps checking whether you have really believed, hear John's words: “Even if our hearts condemn us, God is greater than our hearts, and He knows all things” (1 John 3:20). Such fear can be part of anxiety or a habit of the mind, and that is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust, and if the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Paul says you were once hostile to God, and now you are reconciled. Ask whether you still think of God as someone to be kept at a distance. Ask what new teaching or pressure might move you from the hope you first heard. And thank God that he will present you blameless, because of Christ.

passages.t: Paul's sufferings, and ‘Christ in you, the hope of glory’
passages.happening:
“Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you, and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions for the sake of His body, which is the church” (verse 24).

Paul's task is to “fully proclaim to you the word of God, the mystery that was hidden for ages and generations but is now revealed to His saints” (verses 25-26). And here is the mystery: “the glorious riches of this mystery, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory” (verse 27).

“We proclaim Him, admonishing and teaching everyone with all wisdom, so that we may present everyone perfect in Christ. To this end I also labor, striving with all His energy working powerfully within me” (verses 28-29).
passages.hearers:
‘Mystery’ was a word the Colossians knew. In that world, mystery religions held secret rites that only a few were let into. Paul uses the word differently. The mystery is God's plan, once hidden and now told openly to everyone: that Gentiles, people from every nation, have Christ living in them, and with him the hope of sharing his glory.

Notice the word ‘everyone’, three times in verse 28. The other teaching may have offered a higher life for a spiritual few. Paul's gospel is for everyone, and its goal is to bring everyone to maturity in Christ.

And notice where Paul's energy comes from: ‘all His energy working powerfully within me’. Paul works hard, and it is God's power doing it.
passages.ot:
Daniel spoke of the God who reveals what was hidden: “But there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries” (Daniel 2:28).

The mystery of Gentiles brought in was promised long before. God said to his Servant, “I will also make You a light for the nations, to bring My salvation to the ends of the earth” (Isaiah 49:6).

And the suffering servant of Isaiah stands behind Paul's own sufferings: “Surely He took on our infirmities and carried our sorrows” (Isaiah 53:4). Christ's sufferings saved; Paul's serve the church Christ saved.
passages.hard:
‘I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions.’ Does this mean the cross was not enough?

No. The verses just before say plainly that God has already reconciled the Colossians through Christ's death (verses 20-22). Nothing is missing from what Christ did to save. He offered himself “once for all” (Hebrews 10:10).

So what does Paul mean? Readers explain it in more than one way. Many link it to a Jewish expectation that God's people would pass through a set measure of suffering before the end; Paul gladly takes a share so that the church bears less. Others note how closely Christ is joined to his people: when the risen Jesus met Paul on the road, he asked, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute Me?” (Acts 9:4). So the church's sufferings are, in a real sense, Christ's, and Paul's sufferings for the church belong to them. Others read it as the suffering needed to carry the gospel to the nations, a work Christ began and his servants carry on. These notes do not choose. None of these readings suggests that the cross needs adding to as payment for sin.

And Paul does not say suffering is good in itself. He says that his suffering, for the sake of others, is not wasted.
passages.asks: Paul says the mystery is ‘Christ in you, the hope of glory’. Ask whether you believe Christ lives in you, ordinary as you are. Ask what suffering you carry for the sake of others, and whether you can see it as not wasted. And ask whom you could help grow up in Christ.
